source.title: Learning with Bad Training Data via Iterative Trimmed Loss Minimization

record.tranche_reason: Measures training accuracy over epochs for clean and corrupted samples in deep networks, using the same kind of learning-curve measure as the claim’s real-labels-first version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports noisy-label classification test accuracies for Baseline and ITLM in Tables 1 and 2, but those values do not report training error on completely random labels. The reported results for those methods do not establish fitting random labels, training time relative to clean-label training, or performance on unstructured inputs. Table 3 and Table 4 concern GAN data filtering and backdoor defense, respectively, and do not bear on these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training-accuracy curves for clean and corrupted labels, directly testing the early-learning component of V6 with the same kind of measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: clean samples tend to have higher accuracy or lower loss, especially early in training, motivating iterative filtering and retraining. The authors demonstrate ITLM's utility and provide guarantees for generalized linear models, while leaving the explanation and failure conditions of the neural-network learning dynamics open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a similar training-accuracy-over-epochs observation on clean and bad samples, but studies noisy-label filtering with ITLM rather than reproducing the original studies’ random-label fitting experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says early stopping may help filter bad samples because later rounds may overfit them; the reported training-accuracy comparison is specifically for 40% random label errors on CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: ITLM improves validation accuracy under label corruption, but its reported method comparisons do not establish random-label interpolation or the temporal order of memorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative trimmed-loss training improves classification accuracy under several tested label-corruption conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1(c) compares GAN behavior on two image distributions rather than learning real versus noisy labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GAN training distinguishes majority-distribution images from contaminating images early in training.

record.problems: The relevant learning-curve result is presented as a figure without exact values or uncertainty estimates. The reported comparison covers one stated random-label corruption level and does not show fitting fully random labels.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results meet the row criterion for the claim versions. Noisy-label classification test accuracies in Tables 1 and 2 do not measure the training-error behavior named by V1 or V4.

untested.parts: Training to zero or near-zero error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence time across corruption fractions.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across corruption fractions and the accompanying full test-error trajectory toward chance. Table 1 reports validation accuracy without establishing perfect training fit.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
Eventual memorization of corrupted labels and direct evidence that shared patterns, rather than individual clean examples, account for earlier learning; comparison with fully random labeling.

missing.what: A separate training-accuracy comparison for clean and systematically mislabeled CIFAR-10 samples: the authors explicitly state that clean samples have higher accuracy early in training. Exact numerical values are unavailable.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text does not preserve readable numerical curve values, so the V6 verdicts rest on the authors' explicit qualitative statements. Backdoor experiments deliberately induce a target behavior and do not establish any listed version. The assertion of unpresented Gaussian-noise GAN results does not test V3.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a standard network reaches zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels, with test error at chance and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time factor relative to true labels and how convergence time changes with corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error stays perfect across corruption fractions and whether test error rises steadily toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation affect fitting random labels or generalization on true labels.

The paper measures early accuracy differences between clean and bad samples, but does not report that real-label patterns are learned before random labels are memorized across training, or compare learning of fully random labels.

rows.subject: WideResNet-16
rows.operation_detail: Tracked accuracy on clean and bad training samples over training epochs during naive training on CIFAR-10 with random label errors.
rows.measure: Training accuracy by sample group over epochs; the text states that models are more accurate on good samples early in training.
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative early-epoch comparison but no numeric values. The figure plots clean and bad sample accuracy separately.
rows.check: Change partial to observed: the authors explicitly report higher accuracy on clean samples early in training. Unmeasured later memorization is an untested part, not evidence that the observed early-learning effect is weak. Use corrupted-sample accuracy as the comparison baseline; exact curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.
